narrative:
Based on your academic record and background, the admissions model estimated a 59.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that risk is higher than the chance of passing, the application was denied. This is not a judgment of your character, but rather a prediction based on patterns from past students.

The single strongest factor in this decision was your class ranking in the third year of your undergraduate studies. You placed in the bottom decile, while students who were admitted typically ranked around the sixth decile. This placed you well below the average and pushed the prediction strongly toward bar exam failure. It signals that your academic performance, especially in later years, may not yet reflect the level of mastery needed for law school success.

Your LSAT score also contributed to the risk, though less than your class ranking. At 24, your score was far below the average of 37 among admitted students. This reinforced the prediction toward failure, as lower standardized scores are associated with greater difficulty in the bar exam.

Interestingly, your family income worked in your favor. Coming from a lower-middle income background slightly pushed the prediction toward passing, especially compared to admitted students who were mostly upper-middle or middle income. This may reflect additional motivation or resilience, but it was not enough to offset the other concerns.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retake the LSAT with dedicated preparation. A stronger record and higher score will directly address the two factors that mattered most in this decision.
